title: Why do I procrastinate starting to write? Causes and fixes for Mac writers in 2026
metaTitle: Why do I procrastinate starting to write? Causes and fixes
description: You put off the first sentence because starting feels heavier than editing. Here are the causes, real costs and fixes you can try on your Mac today.
targetKeyword: why do I procrastinate starting to write
intro: You put off writing because the first sentence asks the most from you. Starting means choosing words from nothing, which feels heavier than editing a draft that already exists. This page covers the causes, the real costs, and fixes you can use on a Mac without buying anything.
tldr: Starting feels hard because a blank page asks for topic, order, length and tone all at once.
A 2022 survey of 146 writers found physiological and motivational causes were the most common.
Choose the first action in advance. Ten minutes and one bad paragraph beats waiting to feel ready.
Pages, dictation and a quiet Mac setup lower the cost of starting. Lazur can point, guide and dictate.

blocks.text: Why starting feels harder than carrying on

Starting and continuing feel like different tasks, and they are. Once a draft exists, you edit it. Editing asks less of you than choosing every word from nothing. A blank page asks for the topic, the order, the length, and the tone before you type a word.

That is why the first session is often the hardest. You can sit at your Mac for an hour, open Pages, and write nothing. The file looks ready. You are not. Most people do not avoid writing because they are lazy. They avoid it because the first ten minutes feel bad, and each skip makes the next one easier to excuse.
What the research says about writer's block

One study on this topic is Ahmed and Güss (2022), published in Creativity Research Journal. The authors surveyed 146 writers with a mixed-method online questionnaire. Physiological and motivational causes were the most common. Those causes disrupted composition more often than idea generation did.

What does that mean for you? Your problem may be less about having ideas and more about getting sentences onto the page. Professional and semiprofessional writers reported similar blocks, similar fixes, and similar block lengths. Being paid does not make you immune.
Read this as a map, not a verdict. The study is a survey of what writers said, not a trial of what fixes them. Your own pattern may look different, and that is useful information too.
What avoiding writing costs you in hours and money

The first cost is time. The second is money, if writing is paid work. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a median pay of $36.98 an hour for writers and authors in May 2025. That is the median for the whole occupation, not a promise for your rate. Use it as a yardstick, then swap in your own number.

blocks.caption: Illustrative math at the BLS median hourly pay, not your own rate.

blocks.text: Hours are the real currency here. A skipped session does not vanish. It moves into a later, tighter slot, and that slot often comes with less time and more pressure. Multiply your lost hours by your hourly rate. The number usually looks bigger than the excuse felt at the time.
Costs that do not show up on an invoice

A study on students adds a warning. Tice and Baumeister (1997) found that procrastinators earned lower grades than other students. They also reported higher cumulative stress and illness. I read this through the APS Observer summary, not the original paper, so treat the details as a summary. Students are not writers, so read the link as a signal, not a rule.

APS Observer also reports Ferrari's work, which found that as many as 20 percent of people may be chronic procrastinators. That is a secondary summary, and I did not open the original study. Use the number to see that you are not alone, not to label yourself.
A worked example: the article that never starts

Here is an example, not a case study. A writer has a feature due on Friday. On Tuesday, they open Pages, read the brief, and close the window. On Wednesday, they reorganize a research folder. On Thursday night, they type four sentences and feel worse.

What changed the pattern was a smaller rule, not more willpower. The writer set one first action: write one bad paragraph before touching research. They set a ten minute timer and accepted that the paragraph would be weak. The paragraph was weak. The next one came faster, and the feature was finished by Thursday afternoon.
Mistakes that keep the loop going

items: Waiting until you feel ready. Readiness usually follows the first sentence, not the other way around.
Rereading the brief again and again. Rereading gives you a feeling of progress with no words on the page.
Aiming for a finished draft as the first goal. A finished draft is too far away to start toward on a bad day.
Opening research tabs before the draft. Tabs give your attention an easy exit.
Polishing the first paragraph forever. Editing feels safe, so you stay there.
Planning a three hour block for the first session. Long blocks look productive and feel heavy from the start.

blocks.text: Each of these feels like progress. None of them puts a sentence on the page. If you catch yourself doing one, switch to the first action you wrote down, even if it feels silly.
How to start writing today with no extra tools

Ahmed and Güss (2022) asked writers which solutions worked. Writers described twelve solutions in total. The four solutions writers found most useful were taking a break from writing, working on a different writing project, forcing yourself to keep writing, and discussing ideas with others. None of the four needs an app or a subscription.

Use the break or the different project first when the blank page feels loud. Both lower the stakes without asking for good prose. Use forced writing once you have one sentence on the page and want momentum. Talk an idea through when you know what you want to say but not how to start saying it.
Set the first action before you sit down

Implementation intentions are plans in the form: when this happens, I will do that. Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006) reviewed 94 independent tests with over 8,000 participants. They reported an effect of d = .65 on goal attainment, compared with goal intentions alone. A secondary summary notes that later re-analyses suggest a smaller effect, so expect a modest gain, not a cure.

Try this wording: When I put my coffee down at my desk, I will open the draft and type one sentence in Pages. The trigger and the action should both be specific. A vague plan like I will write more today gives you no starting point at all.
Setting up Pages so starting costs less

Pages is a good place to shrink the cost of starting, because setup takes a few minutes. Check your version first with Pages > About Pages. Apple's Pages guide covers Pages 15.4, so compare your version with that guide before you follow any steps.

Next, check the zoom. Pages > Settings > General holds the default zoom, which Apple lists at 125 percent. The zoom menu runs from 25 percent to 400 percent. A smaller zoom shows more of the page, which can make a long draft look less threatening. A larger zoom helps if small text tires you out.

Use Enter Full Screen to hide the desktop while you write. Pages also offers One Page and Two Pages views, plus tabbed documents, so you can keep the draft in one tab and an outline in another. Apple lists these options in its guide to changing the document view.

Word and Google Docs work the same way. Open one document, close the rest, and type one sentence before you look at anything else. For setup steps in each app, see the [Word guide for writers](/for/writers/word) and the [Google Docs guide for writers](/for/writers/google-docs).
Dictation: speak the rough draft, then edit

Some people freeze at the keyboard and talk easily. In any app, hold fn to dictate text at the cursor. Lazur turns your speech into clean, formatted text. You can add snippets and a personal dictionary for names and phrases you use often. Dictation is unlimited on both paid plans.

Speaking lowers the bar. A spoken first pass sounds like a rough conversation, which is what a first draft needs. Expect mistakes in names, numbers, and quotes. Read those parts back before you trust them. To test how well dictation handles your voice, try the [dictation accuracy checker](/tools/dictation-accuracy-checker).
Where Lazur fits, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a control is, and it draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and it guides you one click at a time.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. You still choose the words and press the keys. Lazur can explain, point, guide, dictate, draft, and handle everyday jobs such as timers and reminders. For prices and the free trial, see the [pricing page](/pricing).
Students and regulated jobs need extra care

Students face graded work, so avoidance shows up in marks as well as stress. Break the assignment into the smallest first action you can name. If deadlines are the real problem, tell your instructor early. Your campus may also have a writing center that helps with drafts.

Lawyers, nurses, accountants, and other regulated professionals must follow their employer's rules on client or patient data. Before you paste a draft into any AI tool, including Lazur, check what your employer allows. Lazur sends audio and screenshots to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Your employer's rules still decide what you may share.
When avoidance needs more than a better routine

If you avoid writing for weeks, cannot start even small tasks, or feel low most days, talk with a doctor or a licensed counselor. Avoidance can travel with stress, poor sleep, or low mood. A better routine can help, but it does not replace care when those problems are real.
Your next step this week

Start small this week. Pick one document and one first action, and write both down before you open the app. Use the same action for three days, even when the writing is poor. Then compare your notes. The fix that got you moving fastest is the one to keep.

faq.question: Is it normal to put off starting to write?
faq.answer: Yes. Most people delay writing at some point, and the usual cause is the first step rather than laziness. Ferrari's work, as summarized by APS Observer, suggests as many as 20 percent of people may be chronic procrastinators. Treat that as a rough signal, not a diagnosis.

faq.question: Is procrastinating on writing the same as writer's block?
faq.answer: Not exactly, but they often show up together. Writer's block usually means you cannot compose or find ideas. Procrastination is the delay itself. Ahmed and Güss (2022) found physiological and motivational causes most common among 146 surveyed writers.

faq.question: Does dictation fix procrastination?
faq.answer: Not on its own. Dictation lowers the cost of a rough first version, which can help a stuck writer speak instead of type. It does not make the decision to start for you. Pair it with a set time and one clear first action.

faq.question: Will Lazur write my article for me?
faq.answer: Lazur can draft text, type it at your cursor, and explain a paragraph out loud. The ideas and the final words should still be yours. Check your school or employer rules on AI help before you submit anything.

faq.question: What if I start and then stop again?
faq.answer: That is normal. Go back to the same document, read the last sentence, and write the next one. Restarting the same way each time makes the start easier to repeat.

faq.question: How long should my first session be?
faq.answer: Start with ten minutes, then decide whether you want more. A short timer lowers the stakes and gives you a clear end. Long blocks can feel heavy when you are stuck.

faq.question: Do I need Pages to use these fixes?
faq.answer: No. The fixes work in any writing app, including Word and Google Docs. Pages gets the setup steps here because it is one common Mac option, and Apple's guide covers Pages 15.4.

faq.question: Can I trust the numbers on this page?
faq.answer: Treat them as starting points. The Ahmed and Güss survey relied on what writers reported. The Gollwitzer and Sheeran figures come from a secondary summary, and later re-analyses found smaller effects. Check the original paper before you quote a number.

costs.title: Hours you do not get back
costs.text: Every skipped session pushes writing into a later, tighter slot. The BLS reports a May 2025 median of $36.98 an hour for writers and authors. At that rate, two lost hours a week is about $74, and five is about $185. Use your own rate if you know it.

costs.title: Rushed drafts and missed deadlines
costs.text: When you start late, you write under pressure. Rushed drafts need more edits, and edits take more hours. A missed deadline can cost a client, an editor, or a grade. Track the cost for one month and you will see the pattern clearly.

costs.title: Stress and illness
costs.text: The APS summary of Tice and Baumeister (1997) reports higher stress and illness among procrastinators than among other students. That study is about students, not writers. Treat it as a warning sign, not a verdict on your health.

costs.title: A flat market for writing work
costs.text: The BLS projects 0 percent employment change for writers and authors from 2025 to 2035, which it describes as little or no change. Demand is not expected to grow enough to cover slow output. If you write for money, your pace is the part you control.

costs.title: The guilt that makes the next start harder
costs.text: Avoidance usually brings guilt, and guilt makes the file feel risky to open. That feeling adds to the next delay, and the loop gets longer each week. These costs do not appear on a timesheet, but they change how the work feels.

causes.title: The blank page is the hardest part
causes.text: Starting asks you to choose words, order, and length from nothing. Ahmed and Güss (2022) surveyed 146 writers and found physiological and motivational causes were the most common. Those causes disrupted composition more often than idea generation did. The problem is often putting sentences down under pressure, not a lack of ideas.

causes.title: Waiting to feel ready
causes.text: Many writers wait for a good mood, a clear head, or a free afternoon before they begin. Those conditions rarely arrive together. Readiness usually follows a first messy sentence, not the other way around. Every day without a start looks like a reasonable day to wait again.

causes.title: Fear of a bad first draft
causes.text: A first draft is supposed to be bad, but many people still expect it to be good. When the gap between that expectation and the blank page feels large, closing the file feels safest. A common explanation is that people delay tasks to avoid the bad feelings the task brings up.

causes.title: A vague first step
causes.text: The goal is a finished article, but the first action is unclear. Opening the document does not tell you what to do next. Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006) tested plans with a specific trigger and action, and reported an effect of d = .65 on goal attainment. The fix is to choose the action in advance.

causes.title: Distraction gives you an exit
causes.text: Email, messages, a research tab, and a tidy folder all offer an easy exit from the blank page. Each one feels like work, and none of them moves the draft forward. On a Mac, that exit is one click away, so your setup matters as much as willpower.

causes.title: Stress feeds the next delay
causes.text: Tice and Baumeister (1997) linked procrastination with lower grades and more stress and illness, as summarized by APS Observer. Stress makes the next task look heavier. A heavier task invites another delay, and the loop can run for weeks.

fixes.title: Write one bad sentence before anything else
fixes.text: Open the file and type one sentence you would never publish. Set a ten minute timer if you need a limit. The goal is to break the blank page, not to finish the section. The second sentence can come easier once the first one is on the page.

fixes.title: Take a break with an end time
fixes.text: In Ahmed and Güss (2022), taking a break from writing was one of the four solutions writers found most useful. Set a short break with a fixed end, such as ten minutes away from the screen. Then return to the same document. An open-ended break turns into another avoidance.

fixes.title: Work on a different project for one session
fixes.text: Writers in the same study also named working on a different writing project as a top solution. Spend one session on a short email or an outline for another piece. Then return to the stuck draft. The switch lowers the pressure without costing you the day.

fixes.title: Force yourself to keep writing for a set time
fixes.text: Forcing yourself to keep writing ranked among the four most useful solutions in Ahmed and Güss (2022). Choose a fixed time, keep typing even when the sentences are poor, and do not reread the last paragraph until the timer ends.

fixes.title: Talk the idea through with someone
fixes.text: Discussing ideas with others was also on that list of four. Tell a colleague, a friend, or a writing group what the piece argues. Say it out loud before you type it. You may hear the first sentence while you explain.

fixes.title: Write an if then plan for the start
fixes.text: Use this form: When [trigger], I will [first action]. Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006) reported an effect of d = .65 on goal attainment, based on 94 tests. Later re-analyses found smaller effects, so expect a modest gain. Example: When I sit down after lunch, I will type one sentence in Pages.

fixes.title: Set Pages up so opening it feels quiet
fixes.text: Use Enter Full Screen to hide the desktop. Check the zoom in Pages > Settings > General, where Apple lists a default of 125 percent. Keep one Pages tab for the draft and close the rest. Fewer open windows means fewer easy exits.

fixes.title: Dictate the rough version
fixes.text: Hold fn and speak the first two paragraphs as if you were explaining them to a friend. Then edit the typed text. For some people, speaking feels less like a test than typing does. Read names and numbers back before you keep them.

plan.label: Morning
plan.title: Choose one document and one action
plan.text: Pick the piece you will work on today. Write down the first action in one sentence, such as Type the opening question. Close other tabs before you start, so the first action is the only option left.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Write the bad paragraph
plan.text: Set a timer for ten minutes. Write one paragraph you would not show anyone. Do not edit it yet. Stop when the timer ends, even if the paragraph feels unfinished.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Use a break with an end time
plan.text: Start with the same first action. When you stall, take a short break with a fixed end. Return to the same document, not a new one, so the session stays connected.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Test an if then plan
plan.text: Write one plan in the form When I, I will. Use the same trigger each day for a week. Note whether you started on the days you planned to start.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Keep the fix that worked
plan.text: Review your notes. Which fix got you into the draft fastest? Make that fix your default for the next piece, and drop the ones that did not help.
